newsitem.title: UK: Second UK barley quality test suggests mixed crop.
newsitem.headline: Second UK barley quality test suggests mixed crop.

text.p: The second interim quality assessment for UK barley suggested a mixed crop with high specific weight and nitrogen content, the Home-Grown Cereals Authority (HGCA) said on Wednesday.
But the results could improve further when spring barley samples were received.

Over 400 barley samples mainly from English winter varieties showed an average nitrogen content of 1.82 percent which is above the five-year average of 1.75 percent but below last year's final average of 1.84 percent, HGCA said.
Generally malsters require nitrogen content of no more than 1.8 percent but HGCA said in recent years brewers had been able to use malting barley with nitrogen up to 1.9 percent.
"The proportion of samples recording less than 1.8 percent nitrogen is so far 51 percent," HGCA said in a weekly digest.
But for varieties approved by the Institute of Brewing the proportion under 1.8 percent was 69 percent.
The Southwest had recorded the lowest average nitrogen content to date at just 1.65 percent, it said.

The average specific weight was the same as the past five year's average at 66.8 kg per hectolitre. The small grains content averaged at 6.4 percent, above the five-year average of 4.9 percent and last year's final of 5.9 percent.
Screening levels were generally higher than last year.

Wheat samples were insufficient to make quality assessments, but 100 results received from East England indicated specific weights above the past five year average at 78.4 percent, low average small grains content and good hagbergs well above millers' minimum requirements.
But the average protein content at 10.2 percent was below the five year average of 10.6 percent, HGCA said.
